segments.text: AI can fake a voice, a face, a video, or a screenshot, cheaply and convincingly.
And it's only getting better.
Knowing fakes exist isn't a skill.
It doesn't tell you what to do in the 10 seconds after a clip hits your feet.
Preventing manipulation requires you to develop a specific, immediate mental reflex the moment
you consume media.
This board compares how we evaluate information across two different eras.
A friend sends you a video of your principal announcing that school is closed next week.
The face, the voice, and the hallway all look right.
On the left, we see the mindset before AI.
You study the pixels to determine the truth.
Because it looks authentic, your call is, I'd believe it.
Now look at the right side.
In the AI era, you ignore the pixels and check the trail.
You find no current closure notice on the school website,
so your call is, I'd wait for the school to confirm it.
Look at the banner at the bottom of the board.
Appearance can mislead.
The source trail can be checked.
The core fake trap is believing a claim simply because it looks real.
There is an inverse trap as well, dismissing the actual truth because it could be a fake.
Some takes are friendly.
A friend might fake a picture of your hockey buddies hoisting the Stanley Cup.
Everyone knows it is fake.
Everyone is in on the joke, and there is no harm done.
This graphic explains harmful fake motives.
Money, power, fame, and cruelty.
Outrage gets pain clicks.
Changing beliefs changes how people vote, protest, and spend.
Viral clips bring fame without truth.
Cruelty exists solely to humiliate, especially at school.
Spiking emotions, outrage, fear, excitement, or hope, is your warning sign.
A strong feeling is your cue to stop and run manual checks.
If you try an AI detector, treat its verdict as a clue, never a ruling.
Those tools make mistakes.
This board outlines a three-step framework for checking clips.
First, the source.
Who posted it?
And do they have a reason and way to know?
Second, context.
One was it recorded and what was said before and after.
Finally, corroboration.
A claim requires an independent source to confirm the event.
Apply these three checks back to the video of the principal closing the school.
Think about how you would verify it.
You go back to the source trail.
Look for the full announcement on the school website and check which dates it covers.
If the dates are unclear, ask the school office using the contact information you already have.
Until the school confirms next week's closure, the claim is unverified.
Verify somewhere at the sender does not control.
If someone posts a fake about you or makes an account pretending to be you, tell an adult you trust.
If it's safe, manually write down the username, the link, and the date so you can report it together.
If someone makes or shares a fake sexually explicit image of anyone under 18,
never screenshot, download, or forward it, even to make a report.
Ask a trusted adult to help you report it through the platform.
NC mex, take it down, and cyber tip line can also help.
Read the text on this final graphic.
Seeing or hearing isn't proof anymore.
Check the source, not the pixels.
